newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 8.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BT RIVALS CHALLENGE PRICE CUTS OF 25 PER CENT

A number of competitors are moving in to outpace British Telecom's price cuts of 25 per cent on domestic and international calls. Energis, the National Grid telecommunications subsidiary, is offering to undercut BT by 50 per cent for selected business customers on direct dialled calls to America. AT&T have said it will continue to undercut basic BT rates in the domestic market by up to 40 per cent. Nynex declared it would match BT cuts. Telewest promised to maintain its 10 to 15 per cent advantage over BT. BT have shrugged off the counter attacks.
-- UNITED UTILITIES AGREES DISPOSAL

United Utilities have agreed a 125 million stg sale of its process equipment division, one of the businesses it put up for sale in March as part of a 350 million stg disposal programme. The California-based water treatment group, United States Filter, is offering 100 million stg in cash and 25 million stg worth of its own shares. However, United Utilities plans to sell the stock in a placing. The final price may be adjusted to reflect net assets on competition.
-- SFO PROBES LAWYERS' HOME LOAN TO YOUNG

The Serious Fraud Office's investigation into whether sacked Morgan Grenfell fund manager Peter Young personally benefited from his own actions will concentrate on the Zurich-based lawyers, Juerg Wyler and Marco Wolf, employed by Mr Young to establish a web of Luxembourg-based holding companies and who lent him the bulk of the money to buy his new home. The exact terms of the loan are not yet apparent to investigators.
THE TIMES
-- BANKS THROW EUROTUNNEL 4.7 BILLION STG LIFELINE

A deal has been reached between bankers and the two chairmen of Eurotunnel to rebuild the company's finances. The deal paves the way for Eurotunnel's shares to resume trading after an eight day suspension. The banks have agreed to cut 4.7 billion stg of high interest borrowing from the company's nine billion stg debt in return for a minimum 45.5 per cent share of the company's equity. If the company performs badly the banks can take a majority share of up to 60.6 per cent by 2003.
-- BOTNAR STRIKES 59 MILLION STG DEAL WITH 'DRACONIAN' REVENUE

The chairman and managing director of Nissan UK, Octav Botnar, has paid 59 million stg to settle an outstanding tax claim. He claims his company was destroyed by a combination of Japanese manipulation and Inland Revenue connivance. The payment settles a claim for 250 million stg against Nissan UK. The Revenue says that warrants for Mr Botnar's arrest remain outstanding.
-- SHELL AND TEXACO PLAN TEN BILLION DOLLAR LINK-UP

Two of the world's largest oil companies, Shell and Texaco, have announced that they are negotiating a possible merger of their downstream operations in America. The deal will involve assets worth more than ten billion dollars and would create America's largest downstream refining operation. Two companies will be created to cover the east and west of the US with a share of the total downstream oil market of about 15 per cent. Analysts say the talks could trigger a wave of similar deals in Europe and America.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BANKERS TO FACE INQUIRY BY IMRO

The investment bank Kleinwort Benson is to be investigated by Imro over allegations that it bowed to political pressures by attempting to stop Mark Horn, one of its senior fund managers raising investment questions about French and South African privatisation stocks. A document addressed to the company's compliance chief Richard Hitchman shows that Kleinwort Benson put "undue interference" on its investment management operations.
-- RETAIL BOOM FAILS TO BOOST FACTORIES

British Government hopes that a retail boom would fuel a recovery in the manufacturing sector have been dashed by a sharp fall in factory production. The Office for National Statistics said that factory output has dropped at the fastest annual rate for over four years. City analysts say the figures highlight the growing distance between a buoyant consumer sector and a gloomy outlook for industry.
-- FORMER BET CHIEF STARTS THREE MILLION STG HIGH-COURT CLAIM FOR SACKING

John Clarke, the former chief executive of services company BET, is to sue Rentokil, the company which bought BET for 2.2 billion stg in April, in a three million stg High Court battle. Mr Clarke is demanding 1.4 million stg for loss of salary plus damages for loss of pension rights, options, bonuses, car and chauffeur and health insurance. The action could destroy the accepted doctrine of "heads rolling" after a hostile bid.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- OFGAS TRIES TO CALM ROW WITH GAS

Gas industry regulator Clare Spottiswoode said she did not intend to accuse British Gas of a personal campaign against her following her outburst against the company last week. Ofgas officials have played down reports that Ms Spottiswoode was pushed into a climbdown by ministers. She pledged that it would be "business as usual" with British Gas, even though the two sides are to fight out the dispute over TransCo price controls before the Monopolies and Mergers Commission for the next six months.
-- SHV LAUNCHES 506 MILLION STG CASH BID FOR CALOR SHARES

The private Dutch company which owns the Makro cash-and- carry chain, SHV, has launched a 506 million stg bid to buy-out the minority shareholders in the bottled gas group Calor which it first bought into nearly ten years ago. The cash bid is being recommended by the two independent directors on the Calor board, Michael Davis and George Duncan, and will include a 40 pence stg dividend payable from the company's own source. The offer will cost SHV 246 million stg.
-- SHARES REACH ANOTHER RECORD

Shares in London have set a new record for the second day running after the Dow Jones index climbed above the 6,000 level for the first time before profit-taking sent it lower again. Market nerves about potential clashes at the Conservative Party conference over interest rates and a new controversy over single European currency took gilts slightly lower. Also the Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer repeated his view yesterday that countries which do not join the single currency should be excluded from Target, the planned payments system for euros.
